questions.q:
Let $n \geq 4$ be a positive integer and let $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ldots . ., \ell_{\mathrm{n}}$ be the lengths of the sides of arbitrary $n$ - sided non-degenerate polygon P. Suppose

\frac{\ell_{1}}{\ell_{2}}+\frac{\ell_{2}}{\ell_{3}}+\ldots \frac{\ell_{\mathrm{n}-1}}{\ell_{\mathrm{n}}}+\frac{\ell_{\mathrm{n}}}{\ell_{1}}=\mathrm{n}

Consider the following statements:
I. The lengths of the sides of $P$ are equal.
II. The angles of $P$ are equal.
III. $\mathrm{P}$ is a regular polygon if it is cyclic.
Then
options: $I$ is true and I implies II
questions.solution:
given : $\frac{\ell_{1}}{\ell_{2}}+\frac{\ell_{2}}{\ell_{3}} \ldots \ldots .+\frac{\ell_{\mathrm{n}}}{\ell_{1}}=\mathrm{n}$ .........(i)
$\therefore$ Use A.M \geq  G.M
We get
$\frac{\left(\frac{\ell_{1}}{\ell_{2}}+\frac{\ell_{2}}{\ell_{3}} \ldots \ldots+\frac{\ell_{n}}{\ell_{1}}\right)}{\mathrm{n}} \geq \sqrt[n]{\frac{\ell_{1}}{\ell_{2}} \cdot \frac{\ell_{2}}{\ell_{3}} \ldots \cdots \frac{\ell_{\mathrm{n}}}{\ell_{1}}}\therefore \frac{\mathrm{n}}{\mathrm{n}} \geq 1\Rightarrow \mathrm{n}=\mathrm{n}$ So $\mathrm{A} \cdot \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{G} \mathrm{M}$
Hence $\frac{\ell_{1}}{\ell_{2}}=\frac{\ell_{2}}{\ell_{3}} \ldots \ldots \ldots .=\frac{\ell_{\mathrm{n}}}{\ell_{1}}=\mathrm{k}\begin{array}{l}
\Rightarrow \mathrm{k}=\frac{\ell_{1}+\ell_{2} \ldots \ldots+\ell_{\mathrm{n}}}{\ell_{2}+\ell_{3} \ldots \ldots+\ell_{\mathrm{n}}+\ell_{1}}=1 \\
\Rightarrow \ell_{1}=\ell_{2} \ldots \ldots=\ell_{\mathrm{n}}
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Two students $\mathrm{P}$ and $\mathrm{Q}$ perform an experiment to verify Ohm's law for a conductor with resistance $\mathrm{R}$. They use a current source and a voltmeter with least counts of $0.1 \mathrm{~mA}$ and $0.1 \mathrm{mV}$, respectively. The plots of the variation of voltage drop $(\mathrm{V})$ across $\mathrm{R}$ with current (I) for both are shown below
The statement which is most likely to be correct is:
options: $Q$ has both random and systematic errors.
P has both random and systematic errors.
questions.solution:
For student P:
Data points are scattered irregularly around the straight line → random errors present.
Also, the line does not pass exactly through the origin (expected for Ohm’s law) → systematic error present.
For student Q:
Data points lie almost exactly on a straight line with very small scatter → negligible random error, and systematic shift is absent.
Hence, P has both random and systematic errors → correct option is (4).
